newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sees chance of reviving Mideast talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sees chance of reviving Mideast talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Tuesday he believed there was "a fairly decent chance" of reviving peace talks between Israel and the Palestinians.

At a joint news conference with visiting Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, Clinton gave no explanation for his optimism after his meeting with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday failed to advance the process.

"I would not conclude from the fact that I'm giving very noncommittal answers that we cannot get it (the Middle East peace process) going again. I think there's a fairly decent chance that we can," he told reporters.

Clinton rejected a reporter's suggestion that the United States was losing leverage with Israel, saying, "I wouldn't assume that based on the comments that have been made so far." And he said the next step in trying to revive the Middle East talks, disrupted by Israel's decision to build new Jewish housing in East Jerusalem, would come when a Palestinian delegation visits the White House this week.

"It's going to depend on what it's always depended on ... (and that is) the parties taking responsibility," said Clinton, who has made clear he prefers not to resort to a high-pressure, U.S.-run peace summit just yet. He repeated his promise of recent days that "we're going to do our best to get this thing going again."
He said Netanyahu had reassured him on Monday of Israel's commitment to the Oslo accords, which established a framework for reconciliation between Israel and the Palestinians.

"The prime minister has said repeatedly publicly and said again to me when he was here that even though he did not agree with everything about Oslo, he felt that the Israeli government was bound by it, and he thought that he ought to honour it ... And I believe it remains his position," he said.

Critics charge that fear of offending politically powerful and wealthy American Jewish lobby groups that back Israel has kept Clinton from making the tough moves necessary to rescue the peace process from its current crisis.

Administration officials respond that they are even-handed "facilitators" between Israel and the Palestinians and that it is up to the parties -- not the United States -- to resolve their problems for themselves.
That message was reaffirmed by Clinton earlier on Tuesday. "I want these parties to do what they have to do to get this process up and going again," he said.

He said he was troubled by a fresh outbreak of violence on the West Bank, where Israeli soldiers and Jewish settlers shot and killed three Palestinians and wounded 103 on Tuesday. But he said it should not be permitted to divert attention from getting the negotiations going again because "that's the ultimate resolution of all these things."
The White House appealed for calm on the West Bank, saying violence erodes confidence in the value of negotiations.

"This is a time in which we are trying to build confidence between the parties and violence erodes confidence and reminds us all that ... restoring security is a principal aim of our effort, as well as a negotiating process that has integrity," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Israeli-PLO peace moves have been frozen since March 18 when Netanyahu, defying international appeals, broke ground for new Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem. Palestinians say the construction is designed to pre-empt negotiations on future control of that part of the city.

Hanan Ashrawi, a minister in the Palestinian self-rule authority, met U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross at the State Department on Tuesday. Striking a conciliatory note, she called the meeting "a positive beginning" and said she detected "a sense of commitment to reinvigorate the process."
Ashrawi told reporters she would report back to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat who is expected to send other negotiators to Washington for talks later this week.

"We certainly are against any type of violence, and we do not believe that violations also should be accepted," she said. Ashrawi blamed the crisis on "Israeli settlement policies, Israeli policies in Jerusalem."

In reply to a question, she said that "if there is a need for a (Palestinian-Israeli) summit there will be a summit," but that this was not currently under discussion. "Right now we are here to explore the American ideas," she said.
